source: Nguyen, Gupta, Le (2026) Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Adaptive Test-Time Reasoning (UAB)
finding: A two-phase scheme gives every question a few samples, reads answer disagreement (vote entropy) as a difficulty signal, then spends the rest of a fixed sample budget on disagreeing questions. The phase-1 samples still count in the final vote, so the probe is not wasted. Total samples are fixed, so this is an equal-budget test.
numbers: Five open-weight models 1.5B-27B, five benchmarks, N=4 samples per question default. Gain over uniform allocation +2.3% average (+2.5% on the three main models, better in 14 of 15 settings), up to +5.5% on GSM8K (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama3.2-3B). Gains shrink with budget: at N=16 no setting significantly favors UAB. On two larger models (incl. GPT-OSS-20B) UAB beats uniform but no longer beats the ASC baseline.
limits: Small open models; math and logic benchmarks; sample count not token count (per-sample token cost similar); wall-clock overhead small but real. Gains concentrated at low budgets.
agent_relevance: Closest direct answer to GAP 1: a 2-sample disagreement probe that is reused in the vote improves accuracy at equal total samples. The win is small (about 2-3 points) and vanishes at larger budgets.

source: Nguyen, Gupta, Le (2026) UAB ablations: difficulty signal, K, oracle comparison
finding: Vote entropy with only K=2 phase-1 samples ranked failures better than log-probability signals. K=2 gave the best average gain at N>=12; larger K spends budget the probe does not need. Against an oracle that allocates by annotated difficulty level, the 2-sample signal was competitive or better. The accuracy gain peaked at middle levels, not the hardest: when the right answer is absent from the samples, extra samples do not help.
numbers: Qwen2.5-1.5B, N=4: average accuracy 47.0 (vote entropy) vs 44.4-45.0 for NLL, token variance, max-token-NLL and ANLL signals, 45.0 without uncertainty; AUROC vs phase-1 correctness 0.780 (vote entropy), 0.742 (NLL), 0.688, 0.672, 0.662. MATH500 by level (Qwen2.5-1.5B): UAB minus Uniform = +2.3 (L1), +3.4 (L2), +1.6 (L3), +1.1 (L4), +1.5 (L5); allocated samples rise 2.95 to 4.76 from L1 to L5. Table 5: UAB under-allocates 10.5% of questions vs 14.1% for the annotated-difficulty oracle; over-sampled and correct 75.4% vs 59.8%.
limits: Single small model for the ablation; hardest level shows a smaller gain than the middle levels.
agent_relevance: Closes part of GAP 4 and GAP 7: two samples are enough to rank, but the hardest items are where a cheap probe pays least. Sampling disagreement measures difficulty for this model, not for humans.

source: Pishehvar, Morandi, Viswanathan (2026) Evaluating Escalation Signals for LLM Routing: Targets, Controls, and Five Ways to Fool Yourself
finding: Semantic entropy over k stochastic samples predicts small-model failure well on GSM8K, but the sampling itself can cost more than calling the large model. Routing with k=10 on a 12x size pair costs 1.38x always-large. Break-even needs a cost ratio above 11.1 even at a 10% escalation rate with k=10 (above 14.3 at 30%).
numbers: Gemma-3 1B/12B, GSM8K n=250, k=10: always-small accuracy 0.372, always-large 0.484, oracle 0.572. Semantic entropy AUROC 0.871 [0.820,0.915] for 'small model wrong'; 0.734 for 'needs escalation'. Routed accuracy up to nine points above random escalation at matched cost. Cost per query at r=0.56: k+r=16.7 units vs always-large 12.0.
limits: Cost counted in parameter-count units (not dollars or latency); one small model pair; one benchmark with a real signal; n=250.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for GAP 1: a pre-solve sampling probe is not free. For an API-only agent the probe cost must be counted against the baseline. Break-even depends on the cost ratio of the two actions.

source: Pishehvar et al. (2026) difficulty-baseline control and k ablation
finding: A question-only difficulty score (read from the question string by regex) matched semantic entropy on synthetic arithmetic, so the entropy result added no information there. On real GSM8K, entropy beat difficulty by 0.21-0.31 AUROC. Cutting k from 10 to 5 kept AUROC almost the same; k=3 lost about 0.07.
numbers: Synthetic ladder: difficulty baseline AUROC 0.839 and 0.830 vs entropy 0.830 and 0.867 (differences inside a 0.04 noise floor); on Target 3 baseline 0.791 vs entropy 0.722/0.714. GSM8K Target 2: entropy 0.871 vs raw difficulty 0.649 and calibrated difficulty 0.558. k ablation T2 AUROC 0.791 (k=3), 0.865 (k=5), 0.862 (k=10); at k=5 routing dominates always-large (cost 9.80-11.6 vs 12.0, accuracy 0.508-0.520 vs 0.484); k=10 never competitive. One result did not replicate at n=100.
limits: Difficulty on GSM8K was the benchmark annotation, not a deployable estimator; one model pair; small n.
agent_relevance: Closes much of GAP 4 for a model's own signal: 5 samples were enough, 3 were not. Gives S0 a control: always score a free question-only difficulty estimate next to any sampling signal.

source: Zhai, Li, Xiao, Li, Wang (2026) Adaptive Test-Time Compute Allocation for Reasoning LLMs via Constrained Policy Optimization (AdaCompute)
finding: A gradient-boosted classifier on 16 cheap text features (length, numbers, fractions, multi-step words, one entropy estimate from a single call) predicts the best sample count per question. Under a matched average budget it beats uniform and a prompt-length heuristic and tracks a Lagrangian oracle within about 1 point. Tested with API models (DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o-mini) and Qwen2.5-7B.
numbers: MATH, DeepSeek-V3, B=2.0: ours 0.562 at realized cost 1.87 vs fixed-b 0.517 at cost 2.00, oracle 0.571. B=3.0: ours 0.575 (cost 2.73) vs fixed 0.517 (cost 2.00) vs oracle 0.586. GPT-4o-mini MATH B=2.0: 0.512 vs 0.474. Qwen2.5-7B MATH B=3.0: 0.554 vs 0.491 (+6.4 points). GSM8K DeepSeek-V3: 0.965 vs 0.946. The prompt-length heuristic gained only +0.3 to +1.2 points. Over 91% imitation accuracy; GBM trains in under 1 second on N=200.
limits: Fixed-b is the largest integer budget not above B, so at B=3.0 it uses cost 2.00 while ours uses 2.73: not exactly equal cost (at B=2.0 ours is cheaper and better). Same-distribution 80/20 split of MATH or GSM8K; no cross-dataset test. Oracle labels need Acc(x,b) measured on training questions, an offline cost.
agent_relevance: Best evidence for GAP 1 and GAP 10 with an API-only agent: a cheap text-feature difficulty prior gets within about 1 point of the oracle and gives +4 to +6 points over uniform on MATH at about the same budget. It needs offline labelled data from the same task family.

source: Zuo, Zhou, Zhu (2026) Adaptive Test-Time Compute Allocation with Evolving In-Context Demonstrations
finding: A warm-up round of one sample per question doubles as difficulty estimation: solved queries stop, unsolved ones get more rounds, with demonstrations drawn from related solved queries. Run only through public APIs (Gemini-2.5-flash-lite with and without thinking, GPT-4.1 Mini, GPT-5 Nano). The uniform baseline is matched to the elimination baseline's output tokens.
numbers: R=4 rounds, one warm-up round, P=3 neighbouring shots; benchmarks MATH-500 (500 questions), MinervaMath (272), GPQA-Diamond (198), LiveCodeBench (166), Reasoning Gym hard set (400). The text says it has the highest token efficiency on all benchmarks. Exact per-benchmark numbers are only in figures and were not extracted.
limits: Metric is coverage (pass@k), not single-answer accuracy; numbers read from plots only; gain mixes allocation with the in-context demonstration effect.
agent_relevance: Supports GAP 1 qualitatively for an API-only agent: warm-up is a nearly free probe because its output is kept. Exact savings not verified.

source: Brown, Muppidi, Shahout (2026) Predictive Scheduling for Efficient Inference-Time Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Lightweight predictors (an MLP on transformer hidden states, or a LoRA classifier on question text) estimate reasoning length or difficulty before generation; a greedy batch allocator spreads a fixed token total. Middle layers 12-17 carry the strongest signal.
numbers: GSM8K: up to 7.9 percentage points absolute accuracy gain over uniform budgeting at identical token cost, closing over 50% of the gap to a perfect-foresight oracle.
limits: Hidden-state predictor needs white-box access; the text-only LoRA version is the API-compatible one. One benchmark (GSM8K), one model family (DeepSeek).
agent_relevance: Another equal-token result supporting a difficulty prior; it needs training on the target model's own outcomes.

source: Lugoloobi, Foster, Bankes, Russell (2026) LLMs Encode Their Failures: Predicting Success from Pre-Generation Activations (COLM 2026)
finding: Linear probes on pre-generation activations predict human IRT difficulty well (Spearman 0.83-0.87) and a model's own pass-rate difficulty less well (0.40-0.64). The two are different quantities and drift apart as the model reasons longer. Probe-predicted model difficulty predicts the model's own Maj@5 failures better than human IRT difficulty in every reasoning mode.
numbers: Easy2Hard-Bench AMC subset. GPT-OSS-20B: Spearman between IRT and probe-predicted model difficulty falls 0.65 to 0.45 from low to high reasoning; probe AUROC for Maj@5 failure falls 0.78 to 0.64 (a non-linear MLP probe recovers to 0.76). Length-only baseline Spearman 0.15 (human) and 0.19-0.30 (model).
limits: White-box probes (need activations); math and code only; one post-instruction token position.
agent_relevance: Bears on GAP 7 and 10: S0 must estimate difficulty for the solver in use. Human-difficulty features lose value as the solver gets better at reasoning.

source: Lugoloobi et al. (2026) probe-guided routing and cross-dataset transfer
finding: Routing on probe-predicted success matched the best single model at lower cost. Cross-dataset transfer of probes is uneven: a probe trained on one benchmark loses accuracy on another in several settings. The authors say they do not test cross-domain transfer (math to code) and that routing is limited by the reliability of the success estimate, not by the routing policy.
numbers: MATH: router matches GPT-OSS-20B-high accuracy (92%) at 70% lower cost. AIME 2025: matches the strongest model at 37% lower cost ($1.15 vs $1.75). GSM8K: picks Math-7B (94.5% at $0.34) over GPT-OSS-20B-high (94.4% at $2.4). Table 8 AUROC by train set and test set: one setting scores 0.739 on MATH after training on MATH but 0.515 on GSM8K and 0.643 on AIME (row labels garbled in the text extraction); row averages across settings run 0.56-0.85.
limits: Open-weight models with accessible activations; transfer table covers three math benchmarks only; fixed-k majority voting.
agent_relevance: Bears on GAP 8: a difficulty estimator is task-family and model specific, so it needs re-fitting after a model change.

source: Chollet, Knoop, Kamradt, Landers, Pinkard (2025) ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems
finding: ARC-AGI-2 task difficulty is calibrated by human pass rate. Every task in the final sets was solved by at least two independent humans. The paper reports no per-task correlation between human pass rate and any model's pass rate; it reports subset-level human accuracy matched within 1 point across sets, and model scores near floor.
numbers: 407 participants, 515 sessions, 1,848 test pairs, 13,405 attempts, 62% solved; median 2.3 min per attempt (2.2 min for solved). Final tasks: 2-10 humans each; 75% of attempts per task completed, 66% of attempted test pairs; average completion time 2.7 min. Model baselines (semi-private): o3 (medium) 3.0%, o4-mini 2.4%, o3-mini-high 3.0%, ARChitects 2.5%, Claude 3.7 (8K) 0.9%. No self-reported demographic variable significantly related to performance.
limits: Model scores of 1-3% leave almost no variance to correlate. Public training set not difficulty-calibrated. A web search for a later per-task human-vs-model comparison on ARC-AGI-2 found none; the search quota then ran out, so this is not an exhaustive negative.
agent_relevance: GAP 2: there is no published human-vs-model per-task correlation for ARC-AGI-2 in the founding paper. Rule-count features have not been tested on it.

source: LeGris, Vong, Lake, Gureckis (2024) H-ARC: A Robust Estimate of Human Performance on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus Benchmark
finding: Human difficulty on ARC is graded and not strongly tied to simple grid features. Mean success within three attempts is 76.2% on the training set and 64.2% on the evaluation set; 98.8% of tasks were solved by at least one person.
numbers: 784 participants (training) and 948 (evaluation); about 11.8 and 10.3 participants per task. 5 tasks unsolved by anyone in each set (1.3%). Output grid size vs difficulty: r(398) = -0.16 (training, p=.001) and -0.02 (evaluation, p=.649). Error divergence vs success rate: r = -0.81 (training), -0.88 (evaluation). Correlation of people's and machines' error edit-distance profiles about 0.25 (GPT-4o 0.19, Claude 3.5 0.20): people and machines make different errors.
limits: Mechanical Turk adults; three-attempt rule; compared with GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 only on error type, not on per-task rank.
agent_relevance: Gives a per-task human difficulty table for ARC-AGI-1 that could be tested against model pass rates; the paper does not report that. Grid size, the simplest perceptual feature, is a weak predictor of human difficulty.

source: Wang (2026) Humans Disengage, Reasoning Models Persist: Separating Difficulty Registration from Deliberation Allocation
finding: On H-ARC items, reasoning-model trace length follows the human ordering of items by solving time, but only weakly. Inside an item, failed model attempts are longer than successful ones, while successful human attempts are longer than failed ones. Trace length is a weak difficulty cue across items and an error cue within an item.
numbers: Five thinking models with reported ratios: Spearman between trace length and human reaction time across H-ARC items 0.16-0.30 (p<.001); DeepSeek-V3 (non-thinking) -0.05. 400 items, 4,091 human trials. Wrong-minus-right log-duration effect d>0 for all five models (for example d=+0.95 and +1.47) vs d=-0.10 for humans; item-fixed-effects interaction -0.66 log units (95% CI -0.81 to -0.50, n=5,728). Failed traces contain 0.43 more hedge words after controls.
limits: Open-weight thinking models; token counts from each model's native tokenizer; H-ARC only for the primary test.
agent_relevance: Partly answers GAP 6 and GAP 2: the reasoning-token count of a first attempt is available through an API but correlates only 0.16-0.30 with human item difficulty. Within one item, a long trace signals failure, which can serve as a stop-or-escalate cue.

source: Pendharkar (2026) Structural Grid Descriptors Predict Within-Task Solver Success on ARC-AGI
finding: For two symbolic ARC solvers (beam search and stochastic DFS, not LLMs), simple grid-structure descriptors measured halfway through a run separate success from failure within the same task. Most of the signal sits on one grid-complexity axis. A feature frozen on one solver transfers to the other, and an early-stop rule at 50% of the run saves compute.
numbers: 44,800 runs, 400 ARC tasks, 28 configurations per solver. Mean within-task best-feature AUC 0.885 (in-sample); pre-registered held-out set of 41 reliable tasks AUC 0.765 (95% CI 0.717-0.810); cross-solver transfer AUC 0.747-0.762 in four directions; only about 30-40 reliable tasks per solver drive the result. Early stopping at 50%: saves 33.6% of beam-search compute at 98.9% of solve rate kept; on SDFS, detecting degenerate trajectories saves 65.3% at zero solve-rate cost. On 229 of 400 evaluation tasks the DSL gives no valid first step.
limits: Symbolic solvers over a fixed DSL, not LLMs; within-task (not across-task) signal; single author; many results in-sample.
agent_relevance: Tests GAP 6 with a process signal rather than a feature count: mid-run state predicts success and transfers across two search algorithms, but nobody has run it on LLM agents. Rule-count features were not compared.

source: Embretson and Daniel (2008) Understanding and quantifying cognitive complexity level in mathematical problem solving items (Psychology Science Quarterly 50(3), 328-344)
url: Psychology Science Quarterly 50(3) 328-344 (PDF text read from a local copy saved by an earlier pass)
finding: In a primary Embretson application to operational GRE quantitative items, a cognitive-complexity model explained about half of item difficulty by both hierarchical regression and the LLTM. Generating equations and extensive processing of distractors were the only variables significant in both difficulty estimates. The authors say higher prediction is reported only for items made by varying features of an item model.
numbers: 534 undergraduates, eight forms of 43 items; 112 Problem Solving items, 11 dropped for difficulty out of range, 101 analysed. Hierarchical regression R2 = .451 (item-bank difficulty) and .435 (sample difficulty) after five stages (encoding, integration, planning, execution, decision); encoding alone .126 and .107. LLTM delta fit index .724 (comparable to a multiple correlation). Sample difficulty vs bank difficulty r = .834. Correlation between the two proposed sources of complexity r = .255.
limits: One test, one population; coefficients differed in significance across the two difficulty estimates; fit is in-sample (no held-out check reported).
agent_relevance: Closes the numbers part of GAP 5 for one Embretson paper: about 45% R2 in-sample on real items, in line with the text-model review mean R2 .478. The 1995 and 1998 papers were not opened.

source: Carpenter, Just, Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures: a theoretical account of the processing in the Raven Progressive Matrices Test (Psychological Review 97(3), 404-431)
finding: Founding numbers confirmed in the original text. The count of rule tokens in a problem accounted for 57% of the variance in mean error rate across 32 classified problems (45% if constant rules are counted). Mean correct response time correlated .87 with error rate across items.
numbers: Experiment 1a: 12 Carnegie Mellon college students, 34 of 48 Raven items shown (32 classified in the taxonomy). 57% variance from total number of rules; 45% when constant rules are included; r = .87 between mean correct times and errors. Experiment 1b: 22 students. The Tower of Hanoi study used 45 students.
limits: 12 students and 32 items; in-sample fit of one regression; a college sample. No larger-sample replication of the 57% was found in this search (not exhaustive; web quota ran out).
agent_relevance: Settles the unchecked weak spot: 57% and .87 are correct as quoted, but come from 12 people and 32 items.

source: Ge, Kryvosheieva, Fried, Girit, Hariharan (2026) Agent Psychometrics: Task-Level Performance Prediction in Agentic Coding Benchmarks (COLM 2026)
finding: IRT with task features (embeddings, or LLM-as-judge ratings of issue text, repository, solution and tests), plus a split of agent ability into LLM and scaffold parts, predicts task-level success for new tasks, new agents and, more weakly, new benchmarks. The held-out benchmark case shows the cross-benchmark drop.
numbers: New tasks (AUC-ROC, 5-fold CV), baseline / embedding / LLM-judge / combined / oracle: SWE-bench Verified 0.718/0.825/0.842/0.843/0.945; SWE-bench Pro 0.657/0.756/0.744/0.750/0.918; GSO 0.714/0.771/0.769/0.781/0.914; Terminal-Bench 2.0 0.734/0.795/0.805/0.807/0.932. New benchmark (train on three, test on the fourth): SWE-bench Pro baseline 0.571, embedding 0.667, LLM-judge 0.696, combined 0.674, oracle 0.913; GSO baseline 0.637, 0.724/0.743/0.719, oracle 0.912. New agents: IRT-Agent 0.930 vs baseline 0.852 on SWE-bench Verified (oracle 0.949).
limits: Needs response data from many agents to fit; coding agents on fixed benchmarks; ridge regression on frozen scores.
agent_relevance: Bears on GAP 8: a difficulty prior fitted on other benchmarks gains about 0.09-0.12 AUC over the base rate but sits far below an oracle. The authors call it 'a coarse first estimate'.

source: Song et al. (2025) IRT-Router: Effective and Interpretable Multi-LLM Routing via Item Response Theory (ACL 2025)
finding: IRT with BERT query embeddings models each query's latent attributes and each LLM's multidimensional ability, and picks the LLM per query under a cost weight. A semantic-similarity warm-up helps unseen queries. It is an IRT-based allocation example, but it routes across models, not reasoning depth.
numbers: 20 LLMs, 12 datasets. In-distribution: average accuracy 3% above GPT-4o alone at 1/30 of its total cost. Out-of-distribution: performance 2% above the best baseline.
limits: Routes across models, not thinking budget; gains stated against chosen baselines; abstract and results text read, tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Part of GAP 9: IRT difficulty is used for routing in 2025-2026, but not found for reasoning-budget allocation inside an agent loop.

source: Sam, Finzi, Kolter (2025) Predicting the Performance of Black-box Language Models with Follow-up Queries (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: For API-only models, answers to a fixed set of follow-up questions asked after the first answer give features that predict whether that answer was correct, better than logits, self-reported confidence, self-consistency and semantic entropy on reasoning tasks. More follow-up questions help with diminishing returns; they run in parallel.
numbers: AUROC for correctness: GSM8K GPT-3.5 0.7748 (follow-up features) vs 0.7495 (semantic entropy) and 0.5227 (self-consistency); GPT-4o-mini 0.7319 vs 0.5546. CodeContests GPT-3.5 0.6800 vs 0.5346; GPT-4o-mini 0.7924 vs 0.5604. Pre- and post-answer verbal confidence 0.42-0.55 (chance). Approximating probabilities by sampling instead of top-k log-probs loses under 2 AUROC points.
limits: Needs a linear predictor trained on labelled data for each model; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o-mini only; predicts correctness of a finished answer, not the difficulty of a fresh problem.
agent_relevance: GAP 6 in part: an API-only agent can read post-answer reliability from follow-up questions (about 0.73-0.79 AUROC on reasoning) but verbal confidence is at chance. This reads correctness, not pre-solve difficulty.

source: Wu, Xie, Zhang, Xiao (2026) CODA: Difficulty-Aware Compute Allocation for Adaptive Reasoning
finding: Uses the group success rate from rollouts as an in-policy difficulty signal during RL training and gates a length reward by it. It is a training method, not a scaffold. The difficulty variable is the model's own pass rate, not a feature model.
numbers: Qwen3-8B-Base: on easy tasks (GSM8K, MATH) token cost cut by over 60% with accuracy kept; on hard tasks (AIME24/25) more tokens are spent (Figure 1 token-ratio changes range from -68% to +35% vs GRPO).
limits: Requires RL training; unusable by an agent that cannot train. Accuracy tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Boundary for GAP 9: the mainstream allocation signal is estimated pass rate, not IRT feature models.

source: Kassenaar, Yang, Francois-Lavet (2026) Learning When to Think: Adaptive Reasoning for Test-Time Compute Allocation
finding: A 1.5B distilled model learns by GRPO to choose NoThink, Short or Long as its first token. The brief modes end up more accurate than Long, which shows sorting by difficulty rather than random choice. Mean length falls 41% on MATH500 with a small accuracy loss and the policy transfers to GSM8K.
numbers: MATH500: accuracy 0.782 vs 0.796 base; mean response 4,796 to 2,811 tokens (-41%), averaged over 3 seeds; GSM8K -76% tokens at higher accuracy than baselines at similar length.
limits: Small model; training required; one training set (MATH).
agent_relevance: Another training-based example for GAP 9: first-token difficulty choice is learnable but not by a scaffold alone.
